source.title: Tight bounds for minimum l1-norm interpolation of noisy data
source.authors: Guillaume Wang; Konstantin Donhauser; Fanny Yang

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports theoretical and simulation results on prediction error as feature dimension grows for minimum-l1-norm interpolation, a different model class and method from deep-network double-descent studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports prediction-error bounds and dimension-sweep simulations for basis pursuit, including results in the overparameterized regime. It does not measure a full curve through the interpolation threshold. Figure 1b also reports prediction error over noise levels. Results cited from other work are context, not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper proves and simulates that basis pursuit (minimum-ℓ1-norm interpolation) error falls as d/n grows in sparse linear regression, for d well beyond n. That bears on V4's second descent in a non-deep model class. It does not trace the peak or the curve below the interpolation threshold, and its own aim is consistency rather than double descent, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors prove matching bounds of order σ²/log(d/n) for basis pursuit with isotropic Gaussian features and sparse ground truth. This gives the first asymptotic consistency result for a minimum-norm interpolator on isotropic features and disproves the conjecture of Chinot et al. They conclude that error decays with d/n, so basis pursuit benefits from the regularizing effect of high dimensionality, though only at a slow logarithmic rate.
record.recipe_differences: The study gives theoretical analysis and simulations of minimum-ℓ1-norm interpolation in sparse linear regression, rather than measuring deep-network error curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The dimension-sweep simulations use Normal, Log Normal, and Rademacher features; the theorem applies to isotropic Gaussian features. Figure 1b varies noise variance.

fits_no_version.finding: At d=20000, n=400, basis pursuit error scales with noise variance σ², while min-ℓ2-norm interpolation error is similar and non-vanishing across σ².
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Minimum-ℓ1 interpolation trades a strong sparsity bias for higher noise sensitivity relative to minimum-ℓ2 interpolation in overparameterized regression.

record.problems: The empirical simulations average over 20 runs; standard deviation is shown for Figure 1b, but pointwise numerical values are not stated in the text. The theorem is restricted to sparse ground truth, isotropic Gaussian features, and a specified range of d and n.
record.rows_left_out: No separately cited findings were included. No other result bearing on the tested version was reported beyond Theorem 1 and Figures 1a–1b.

untested.parts: The peak at the interpolation threshold (d≈n), the under-parameterized classical U-shaped segment, and any regime outside κ3 n log(n)² ≤ d ≤ exp(κ4 n^(1/5)). The d≍n non-vanishing lower bound is only cited from other work.
Sample size is fixed in the simulations (n=400); there is no test of more data hurting near the threshold.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Noise is varied only at fixed d=20000, far from the threshold. There is no peak, no multiple descent and no tuned regularization.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3: the paper addresses consistency of basis pursuit, not double descent as such. Row r1 is a theoretical bound rather than an empirical measurement. Rows r2–r4 values are read from Figure 1a only; no pointwise numbers are given. The cited lower bound σ²n/(d−n) for d≍n (from ZSS20 and MVSS20) is context, not a result of this study, so it is not a row.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-wise double descent is not tested.
The number of training samples is not varied to test whether more data can raise test error near the interpolation threshold.
The reported results concern minimum-l1-norm interpolation in the overparameterized regime; they do not trace the curve through the interpolation threshold or test the classical U-shaped portion.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper varies noise level in one simulation but does not test whether noise drives a double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a peak.
The paper does not test whether counting effective parameters turns a second-descent curve into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

conditions.value: n ≥ κ₂ and κ₃ n log(n)² ≤ d ≤ exp(κ₄ n^(1/5))

rows.value: Matching upper and lower bounds of order σ²/log(d/n), exact up to negligible terms when d ≫ n.
rows.note: The result gives the prediction-error rate in the stated overparameterized regime; it does not report a full sweep through the interpolation threshold.

relationships.condition: Basis pursuit, isotropic Gaussian features (theorem) and Normal, Log Normal and Rademacher features (simulation), sparse ground truth, d ≫ n
relationships.reason: Matching bounds of order σ²/log(d/n) show risk falling as overparameterization grows (r1), and dimension-sweep simulations follow this trend (r2–r4). The decay is only logarithmic, which the authors call a tempering result.
relationships.display_finding: Matching risk bounds scaled as σ²/log(d/n), establishing logarithmic improvement with increasing overparameterization that dimension-sweep simulations also followed.
